persona_summary: I am a cryptographer focused on the FORMAL PROPERTIES of hybrid-signature combiners — non-malleability, strong unforgeability (SUF-CMA), commitment to message + algorithm + key, weak vs strong non-separability, BUFF properties. I am NOT a PQ-skeptic, NOT an audit-discipline skeptic, NOT a wire-size pragmatist. My concern is exclusively the COMPOSITION's mathematical properties: when you write `hybrid_sig = ml_dsa_sig || ed25519_sig` with both halves signing the same M' = Prefix || Label || len(ctx) || ctx || PH(M), what does the resulting object provably guarantee, and what does it provably NOT guarantee? My adversarial position is that the public blog draft (Section 2.1 'Strip-resistance' bullet + Section 5 'what we shipped') uses the phrase 'strip-resistant' and 'committing' WITHOUT the qualifiers the LAMPS construction itself attaches to those terms — the LAMPS draft says explicitly that the construction provides only WEAK non-separability (not strong), is only EUF-CMA secure (not SUF-CMA, and the draft itself says applications requiring SUF-CMA SHOULD NOT use Composite ML-DSA), and that 'replacing an ML-DSA signature with a Composite ML-DSA signature is a reduction in security' against quantum adversaries. The blog cannot publish those phrases without those qualifiers; the correct framing is meaningfully weaker than the current draft implies.
evidence_base_verified: LAMPS draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 §Security Considerations (live-verified 2026-05-26 via WebFetch on github.com/lamps-wg/draft-composite-sigs main): 'Composite ML-DSA will be EUF-CMA secure if at least one of the component algorithms is EUF-CMA secure and PH is collision resistant.' Note: EUF-CMA, NOT SUF-CMA. The draft scopes its strong guarantee at EUF-CMA only.

LAMPS draft §Security Considerations (same source, live-verified): 'Composite ML-DSA will not be SUF-CMA secure' against quantum adversaries, and 'applications where SUF-CMA security is critical SHOULD NOT use Composite ML-DSA.' This is the draft authors' own warning.

LAMPS draft §Security Considerations (same source, live-verified): 'none are SUF-CMA secure against a quantum adversary' and 'replacing an ML-DSA signature with a Composite ML-DSA signature is a reduction in security.' Pure ML-DSA-65 standalone is strictly stronger on this axis than the composite that wraps it.

LAMPS draft §Security Considerations: 'weak non-separability' defined as 'the guarantee that an adversary cannot simply remove one of the component signatures without evidence left behind' — the static Prefix CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025 remains as cryptographic evidence that splitting occurred. NOTE the qualifier 'weak'; the draft does NOT claim strong non-separability. This is the formal mechanism: it defends against passive splitting (downgrade-by-stripping where the receiver doesn't notice), NOT against an adversary who can produce a fresh single-algorithm signature on the SAME M that an honest signer also signed via the composite construction.

LAMPS draft §Security Considerations: 'key reuse MUST be avoided to prevent the introduction of EUF-CMA vulnerabilities.' If the user reuses the underlying Ed25519 or ML-DSA-65 key for ANY OTHER purpose (standalone signing, a different composite combination, a different protocol's signing key) the EUF-CMA guarantee of the composite collapses. This is a deployment hazard the blog does not surface.

LAMPS draft M' construction verified: M' := Prefix || Label || len(ctx) || ctx || PH(M) where Prefix = ASCII 'CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025' (hex 436F6D706F73697465416C676F726974686D5369676E61747572657332303235). Signature value = mldsaSig || tradSig (3309 + 64 = 3373 bytes; per Agent-2 §A.1 — note Agent-2 reports 3409 elsewhere; one or both numbers needs cite-grep-verify pre-publication — flagging as a minor finding).

Bindel-Hale, 'A Note on Hybrid Signature Schemes' (IACR eprint 2023/423, July 2023): the FOUNDATIONAL paper showing that naive concatenation hybrid combiners that sign the SAME M with both halves do NOT preserve strong unforgeability. The paper proposes a CORRECTED construction that binds the second (PQ) signature to the concatenation of M and the first (classical) signature — sig2 = Sign(skPQ, M || sig1) rather than sig2 = Sign(skPQ, M). The corrected construction makes overall SUF-CMA depend only on SUF-CMA of the second component. LAMPS does NOT use this construction; LAMPS signs M' with BOTH halves independently. This is by design (interoperability with separately-verifiable component signatures) but it is the explicit reason the LAMPS draft itself disclaims SUF-CMA.

Bossuat-Dottling-Schmieg-Stebila-Tessaro et al., 'Bird of Prey: Practical Signature Combiners Preserving Strong Unforgeability' (IACR eprint 2025/1844, published Feb 2026 — ~3 months before this lens dispatch; will appear in Springer's CRYPTO 2026 / ASIACRYPT 2025 proceedings volume per the link.springer.com chapter assignment): explicitly states 'a simple combiner for signature schemes can be obtained by concatenating the signatures of both schemes, which preserves unforgeability of the underlying schemes, [but] it does not extend to stronger notions such as strong unforgeability.' Proposes three practical combiners (one specifically for EdDSA + ML-DSA, the EXACT pair Benten ships) with SIGNATURE SIZES SMALLER than naive concatenation. This paper is in print as of the dispatch date and is the canonical academic source any cryptographer reviewing Benten's blog will cite.

draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs (CFRG individual submission, in active development 2025-2026): 'design strengthens the property so that SUF-CMA of the overall construction depends only on the SUF-CMA of the second component, regardless of the security level of the first one.' This is the IETF/CFRG community's response to the gap LAMPS leaves open — there is an active draft to standardize a SUF-CMA-preserving alternative.

draft-ietf-pquip-hybrid-signature-spectrums (IETF PQUIP WG): the WG-blessed framework for classifying hybrid signature constructions by which properties they preserve. The LAMPS construction sits in the 'EUF-CMA-preserving + weak-non-separable + committing-via-prefix' cell of that spectrum — explicitly NOT the 'SUF-CMA-preserving + strong-non-separable' cell that Bindel-Hale + Bird-of-Prey + draft-prabel target.

X-Wing KEM combiner (Barbosa/Connolly/Duits/Schwabe/Schmieg/Stebila, IACR Communications in Cryptology 2024-1-21, published 2024-01-21): peer-reviewed academic paper on the X-Wing combiner with formal IND-CCA2 proofs in the QROM, X-Wing-specific transformation properties, and ciphertext-binding analysis. This is the GOLD STANDARD for what cryptographic-combiner peer-review depth looks like (per Agent-2 §C.2). LAMPS composite-sigs combiner has WG analysis from the LAMPS Working Group + the disclaimers above — solid engineering work, but NOT an IACR-peer-reviewed paper of equivalent depth on the SIGNATURE combiner construction. The asymmetry is real (Agent-2 §A.1 acknowledges it; the strategy doc Section 2.2 caveat #2 mentions 'LAMPS draft is in RFC Editor Queue, not yet RFC' but does NOT mention the analytical-depth asymmetry; that omission is the load-bearing surface my lens points at).

per_path.path: F4 — LAMPS WG mailing list engagement (adopter perspective)
per_path.rationale: Mixed exactly the way L2 reads it, with one L12-specific sharpening: positioning Benten as a published adopter REINFORCES the perception that the LAMPS combiner's SUF-CMA-omission is an acceptable trade-off for production-deployment use cases. It is acceptable for X.509/CMS workflows (the LAMPS target context) where signatures are typically over certificate bodies that already have collision-resistant content addressing built in; it is LESS obviously acceptable for content-addressed P2P graph artifacts where signature non-malleability could matter (e.g. an adversary substitutes a different valid composite signature for the same M issued by the same key, breaking the 'this exact signature is the unique authorization token' invariant — this is the SUF-CMA failure class). The LAMPS WG mailing list is the right place to raise the question 'does composite-sig SUF-CMA failure matter in P2P content-addressed deployment, and if so, should the spec recommend Bird-of-Prey-style constructions for that class of adopter?' — that is a genuine WG-useful contribution from an adopter perspective. per_path.path: F5 — Blog post on benten.computer/blog (load-bearing primary signal)
per_path.rationale: This is where the L12 lens has SHARPEST objection — strong recommendation to REVISE the blog draft's specific cryptographic-property claims before publication. The current Section 2.1 ('Strip-resistance of LAMPS construction: forging requires breaking BOTH halves') and the implied Section 5 'what we shipped' framing are NOT what the LAMPS draft itself says. Specifically, three load-bearing problems any cryptographer-reviewer will publicly flag: (1) The phrase 'strip-resistance' without qualifier conflates the property LAMPS provides (WEAK non-separability, against PASSIVE downgrade-by-stripping where receiver doesn't notice the Prefix evidence) with the property LAMPS does NOT provide (STRONG non-separability + SUF-CMA-preservation, against an active adversary who can produce a fresh valid composite signature on the same M given a previously-seen composite signature). The blog needs the precise qualifier: 'strip-resistant against passive downgrade-by-stripping (the static CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025 Prefix leaves evidence; see LAMPS §Security Considerations definition of weak non-separability), NOT strip-resistant against the broader malleability class — see honesty caveats.' (2) The blog's implied claim that the combiner is 'committing' needs the same precision: yes, both halves verify against the SAME M' that includes Prefix + Label + ctx + PH(M), so the combiner commits to algorithm-ID + ctx + message — but it does NOT commit to the COMPOSITE SIGNATURE BYTES (i.e., given a valid composite_sig = mldsaSig || tradSig for message M from key K, an adversary with no secret material may or may not be able to produce a different valid composite_sig' for the same M from the same K depending on the malleability properties of the underlying ML-DSA-65 and Ed25519 implementations — this is the SUF-CMA question that LAMPS explicitly disclaims). The blog should NOT say 'committing' without specifying what is committed. (3) The 'forging requires breaking BOTH halves' claim is true for FORGERY-FROM-ZERO (no prior signatures from key K observed) but is FALSE for SUF-CMA-style attacks where the adversary has seen a valid signature and tries to derive a related one — the LAMPS draft says explicitly 'Composite ML-DSA will not be SUF-CMA secure' against quantum adversaries, and even pre-quantum the SUF-CMA preservation is not formally established for the LAMPS construction as it is for the Bird-of-Prey constructions (eprint 2025/1844). PURSUE the blog WITH the framing-revisions enumerated in specific_blog_text_changes_requested below; otherwise DO NOT PUBLISH. The cost of revision is small (~6 specific text replacements + 1 new honesty caveat #7); the cost of publishing with the current framing and being publicly corrected by a Bird-of-Prey author or LAMPS WG participant is high.

This converts 'we shipped' from a claim into a falsifiable artifact. (b) Include in the library's README a Security Considerations section that mirrors the LAMPS draft's own caveats verbatim — EUF-CMA-only, weak non-separability, key-reuse-prohibition, SUF-CMA-sensitive-applications-SHOULD-NOT-use. This is what a careful crypto-library README looks like (ring, dalek, libsodium all do this); shipping the library without it would invite the exact public correction the blog risks. (c) Include in the library's docs an explicit pointer to Bird-of-Prey (eprint 2025/1844) and draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs as ALTERNATIVE constructions that preserve SUF-CMA, so that adopters choosing between Benten's library and a future SUF-CMA-preserving alternative can make an informed choice. The library is the place where L12's concerns become CONSTRUCTIVE: it lets the wider crypto community help find issues in the combiner implementation BEFORE v1-beta scales, AND it positions Benten as a careful steward of cryptographic detail (not a small team that publishes confident claims without engaging the academic literature).

per_path.rationale: Critical and L12-supportive. The iroh / Signal / MLS / Veilid teams include cryptographers who track exactly the SUF-CMA-vs-EUF-CMA distinction and will read Benten's framing through that lens. Reaching out privately BEFORE the blog publishes gives those teams a chance to push back on the framing (or confirm it) in a context where Benten can absorb the feedback without public retraction. Framing matters: NOT 'validate our deployment,' INSTEAD 'help us think about whether the SUF-CMA-omission of the LAMPS construction is a v1-beta-acceptable trade-off vs needing to track a SUF-CMA-preserving alternative for v1-GM or post-v1.' cross_path_synthesis.summary: From the combiner-soundness-cryptographer persona, 6 of 7 PURSUE-set paths are net-positive AS LONG AS the blog framing (F5) is revised to use the correct LAMPS-aligned cryptographic-property qualifiers + adds a new honesty caveat #7 disclosing the EUF-CMA-only / SUF-CMA-omitted status of the construction Benten ships. The blog is the load-bearing artifact: if it claims 'strip-resistance' and 'committing' without the qualifiers LAMPS itself attaches to those terms, any cryptographer who reads the post + opens the draft-19 spec + reads the Security Considerations section will publicly correct the framing — and the correction is in print (Bird-of-Prey eprint 2025/1844, published 3 months before this dispatch) which makes the correction harder to absorb than 'we'll update v2 of the blog.' If the framing revisions land, the slate is sound. Important: NONE of my objections argue against shipping the LAMPS combiner — it IS the correct choice for Benten's deployment given the absence of a CFRG/IETF-blessed SUF-CMA-preserving alternative + the LAMPS construction's RFC-Editor-Queue maturity + the IANA-allocated OID. My objection is exclusively that the BLOG OVERSTATES the formal properties of the construction Benten shipped, and the LAMPS draft + Bird-of-Prey paper + draft-prabel give the wider crypto community the receipts to push back. Section 4 of the strategy doc anticipates L12 at LOW priority with the steelman 'more-precise language in §5'; that anticipation is structurally correct but undersized — the actual evidence base (LAMPS draft Security Considerations + Bird-of-Prey publication date + draft-prabel existence) escalates this from a cosmetic-wording finding to a substantive accuracy finding.
convergence_with_other_lenses: L2 (PQ-skeptic cryptographer): aligns on the distinction between ALGORITHMIC failure of one half (which the hybrid combiner protects against) and IMPLEMENTATION-or-SUF-CMA failure (which the combiner does NOT protect against). L2's contribution is the SCA literature + the unaudited-substrate framing; L12's contribution is that even WITHOUT any implementation flaws or side-channel leakage, the COMBINER'S FORMAL PROPERTIES are weaker than the blog claims (EUF-CMA-only; weak non-separability; SUF-CMA-omitted by design). Together L2 + L12 give the orchestrator a complete picture: 'the construction is unaudited (L2) AND its formal properties are narrower than the blog framing implies (L12).' Both should be addressed in honesty caveat #3 (L2) + new honesty caveat #7 (L12).

L10 (audit-discipline skeptic): aligns on the 'protects against ALGORITHMIC weakness, not IMPLEMENTATION weakness' framing. L12 extends this to 'protects against ALGORITHMIC FORGERY (EUF-CMA), but does NOT protect against ALGORITHMIC NON-MALLEABILITY (SUF-CMA) per the LAMPS draft itself.' L9 (LAMPS-WG-participant): aligns on the 'shipping pre-RFC' framing — but L12 sharpens by noting that even after RFC publication, the LAMPS construction is by-design EUF-CMA-only + weak-non-separable; the RFC itself will carry those disclaimers. Waiting for the RFC does NOT close the L12 gap; only revising the blog framing or migrating to a Bird-of-Prey-style combiner (post-v1-beta) closes it. L9's 'commit to RFC-conformance update' is necessary but not sufficient for L12 satisfaction.

L6 (HNDL-skeptic for sigs): partially in tension. L6 argues 'content-addressed systems have STRONGER properties (content-hash binds content; signature is one trust factor),' which is true and SOMEWHAT mitigates L12 — if the content-hash CID already binds the message bytes, then a SUF-CMA-style malleability attack on the signature alone may not be exploitable because the adversary's malleated signature still verifies against the SAME content-CID. L12's response: this depends on whether the signature is being used as 'this exact byte-sequence is a unique authorization token' (where SUF-CMA matters) vs 'someone with key K endorsed this content' (where EUF-CMA suffices). Benten's UCAN / cap-delegation / attribution-frame / atrium-acceptance flows include both shapes; some are SUF-CMA-sensitive (a UCAN proof's signature serves as a unique authorization token), some are EUF-CMA-sufficient (a node-author attribution). The blog should NOT claim 'one combiner serves both' without acknowledging which is which.

L15 (threat-model-boundaries): orthogonal. L15 asks 'why didn't Filecoin/Arweave/git/Sigstore make Benten's choice'; L12 asks 'given Benten made the choice, are the public-facing claims about the chosen construction's formal properties accurate.' Both are reasonable independently.

specific_blog_text_changes_requested.section: Section 2.1 — 'Strip-resistance of LAMPS construction' bullet (current draft)
specific_blog_text_changes_requested.current_implied_text: 'Strip-resistance of LAMPS construction: forging requires breaking BOTH halves (per Agent-2 §A.1: `Prefix || Label || len(ctx) || ctx || PH(M)` with fixed prefix `"CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025"`).'
specific_blog_text_changes_requested.requested_replacement: 'Strip-resistance of LAMPS construction (against passive downgrade-by-stripping): the static `CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025` prefix folded into M\' provides what the LAMPS draft Security Considerations section terms WEAK NON-SEPARABILITY — \'the guarantee that an adversary cannot simply remove one of the component signatures without evidence left behind.\' An adversary who strips the ML-DSA-65 component and presents only the Ed25519 component to a verifier that expects a Composite ML-DSA signature will fail verification (the standalone Ed25519 verifier would also fail, because the Ed25519 component signed M\' containing the composite prefix, not the bare message M). For new (zero-prior-signature) forgery, an adversary needs to break BOTH halves: forge ML-DSA-65 cryptanalytically OR steal that key, AND forge Ed25519 cryptanalytically OR steal that key. NOTE the precise scope: this is EUF-CMA (existential unforgeability against chosen-message attack), NOT SUF-CMA (strong unforgeability — the property that even given valid prior signatures, an adversary cannot produce a DIFFERENT valid signature on the same message from the same key). The LAMPS draft Security Considerations section states explicitly that \'Composite ML-DSA will not be SUF-CMA secure\' against quantum adversaries and that \'applications where SUF-CMA security is critical SHOULD NOT use Composite ML-DSA.\' Bird-of-Prey (Bossuat et al., IACR eprint 2025/1844 / CRYPTO 2026) and draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs propose SUF-CMA-preserving combiner constructions for the EdDSA + ML-DSA pair; we evaluate the trade-off in honesty caveat #7.'

specific_blog_text_changes_requested.requested_new_text: 'The LAMPS Composite ML-DSA construction Benten ships is EUF-CMA-secure under standard assumptions (at least one component EUF-CMA-secure + PH collision-resistant) and provides weak non-separability against passive downgrade-by-stripping (via the static `CompositeAlgorithmSignatures2025` prefix folded into M\'). It is NOT SUF-CMA-secure: the LAMPS draft\'s own Security Considerations section states \'Composite ML-DSA will not be SUF-CMA secure\' against quantum adversaries and warns \'applications where SUF-CMA security is critical SHOULD NOT use Composite ML-DSA.\' This is by-design: the construction signs M\' with both halves independently to preserve component-signature verifiability for the X.509/CMS context that LAMPS targets, which means it inherits malleability properties from whichever underlying algorithm is more malleable. Bird-of-Prey (Bossuat et al., IACR eprint 2025/1844, published Feb 2026; to appear in CRYPTO 2026 proceedings) demonstrates that the simple-concatenation approach to hybrid signature combiners does not preserve strong unforgeability and proposes practical SUF-CMA-preserving constructions specifically for the EdDSA + ML-DSA pair — with signature sizes SMALLER than naive concatenation. The CFRG individual draft draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs is the IETF-side response: it proposes a construction where sig2 = Sign(skPQ, M || sig1), making overall SUF-CMA depend only on SUF-CMA of the second component. Both are real alternatives we considered. We chose the LAMPS construction for v1-beta because (i) the LAMPS OID is IANA early-allocated and the draft is in the RFC Editor Queue (production-ready ecosystem alignment), (ii) the Bird-of-Prey constructions are too fresh (Feb 2026 publication) to assume CFRG/IETF blessing on the specific construction within the v1-beta timeframe, (iii) draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs is an individual submission not yet CFRG-adopted, (iv) Benten\'s predominant signature use case (existential endorsement of content via did:key signatures over content-CIDs) is EUF-CMA-sufficient. For our SUF-CMA-sensitive use cases (UCAN proofs and capability delegations, where the signature serves as a unique authorization token), we treat the SUF-CMA-omission as a residual risk tracked for post-v1-beta migration to a SUF-CMA-preserving combiner when one is CFRG/IETF-blessed. We acknowledge this is a trade-off others may evaluate differently.'

'The LAMPS construction REQUIRES that the underlying ML-DSA-65 and Ed25519 keys not be reused for any other purpose (standalone signing of the bare message M, a different composite combination, or a different protocol\'s signing key). (Per pim-N-cite-grep-verify-at-author-time §3.6j ext.)

specific_blog_text_changes_requested.requested_addition: Add explicit items: (a) IACR-peer-reviewed analysis of the LAMPS composite-sig combiner at depth equivalent to the X-Wing KEM combiner (Barbosa et al. IACR CiC 2024-1-21) — the asymmetry between hybrid-KEM analysis depth and hybrid-sig analysis depth is real and worth flagging publicly; (b) CFRG adoption of a SUF-CMA-preserving hybrid signature combiner draft (Bird-of-Prey or draft-prabel or a unifying construction) so that adopters needing SUF-CMA have a CFRG-blessed migration path from the LAMPS EUF-CMA-only combiner; (c) IETF PQUIP-WG or LAMPS-WG guidance on which application contexts are EUF-CMA-sufficient vs SUF-CMA-sensitive, so that adopter implementations like Benten\'s can correctly attribute application use cases to the appropriate combiner shape.'

objection_1.statement: EUF-CMA-vs-SUF-CMA is a niche cryptographic distinction; the blog audience won't notice the difference, and surfacing it just confuses non-specialists.
objection_1.response: The blog audience explicitly includes cryptographers (Section 2.3 'audience-tailored framings' lists 'Cryptographers' as the first audience). For that audience, EUF-CMA vs SUF-CMA is not a niche distinction — it is the FIRST distinction they will make when evaluating a new hybrid-sig deployment. The LAMPS draft itself surfaces the distinction prominently in its Security Considerations section because the draft authors know their audience needs the warning. Omitting it from the blog reads as 'Benten either doesn't know or hopes the audience won't notice,' both of which are reputation-damaging when the audience does notice (and they will — Bird-of-Prey eprint 2025/1844 is in print as of Feb 2026). Surfacing the distinction in honesty caveat #7 is the cheap correct move: cryptographers respect specs that disclose the formal-property scope honestly + non-specialists skip the caveat as they do other technical caveats.

objection_2.statement: Bird-of-Prey (eprint 2025/1844) was published Feb 2026 — only 3 months before this lens dispatch. It's too fresh to factor into v1-beta architectural decisions; the strategy doc Section 6 chose 'Option α (BEFORE v1-beta tag)' for blog publication, which means the blog ships with the LAMPS construction as-shipped.
objection_2.response: I am NOT arguing that Benten should migrate to a Bird-of-Prey construction for v1-beta. The construction Benten ships (LAMPS Composite ML-DSA) is the correct choice given the IANA OID allocation + draft maturity + Bird-of-Prey freshness; that is a legitimate Ben-decision per Section 6. My argument is about the PUBLIC-FACING FRAMING of the construction that was chosen. The Bird-of-Prey paper is in print; it WILL be cited by anyone reviewing Benten's claims. The blog needs to acknowledge that (i) the LAMPS construction has the formal-property scope the LAMPS draft itself defines (EUF-CMA, weak non-separability), (ii) SUF-CMA-preserving alternatives exist in the academic literature and as a CFRG individual draft, (iii) Benten evaluated and chose the LAMPS construction for the stated reasons. That framing is honest, accurate, and Bird-of-Prey-citation-resistant. Hiding the trade-off invites the public correction; surfacing it pre-empts it.

objection_3.statement: The strategy doc Section 4 anticipates L12 at LOW priority with the steelman 'more-precise language in §5 (strip-resistant against downgrade rather than strip-resistant).' That captures the L12 finding; what more do you want?
objection_3.response: The strategy doc's L12 anticipation is structurally correct but undersized. 'More-precise language' is the right shape; the actual delta is larger than 'add a parenthetical qualifier.' The blog draft outline implies six text changes (enumerated above), one new honesty caveat (#7) of meaningful length (~250 words), one additional caveat (#8) on key-reuse, one wire-size cite-grep-verify, and one Section 8 addition. The strategy doc author wrote 'LOW' before reading the LAMPS draft Security Considerations + the Bird-of-Prey publication date + the existence of draft-prabel-cfrg-suf-hybrid-sigs (the strategy doc references the LAMPS construction's 'committing, strip-resistant' properties without acknowledging that LAMPS itself disclaims SUF-CMA). With those evidence base inputs verified live (2026-05-26), L12 escalates from LOW (cosmetic-wording) to HIGH (substantive accuracy + active-published-counter-evidence). The dispatch slate should reflect this — recommend re-prioritization to MEDIUM-HIGH alongside L2 and L10 for any second-round dispatch on the revised draft.

objection_4.statement: If the LAMPS construction is so problematic, why did the LAMPS WG advance it to RFC Editor Queue?
objection_4.response: It is not 'problematic' — it is APPROPRIATELY SCOPED for the X.509/CMS deployment context that LAMPS targets. In that context (CA-signed certificates, document signatures, code-signing manifests), EUF-CMA is sufficient because the signed content is collision-resistant by construction (certificate body has a unique serial number; document has a unique hash; manifest has a unique build provenance), so SUF-CMA-style malleability of the signature does not break the application invariant ('this principal endorsed this content'). The LAMPS WG knew exactly what they were specifying and the Security Considerations section reflects that. The deployment hazard is in OTHER application contexts — like Benten's UCAN-proof or capability-delegation use cases — where the signature IS the unique authorization token and SUF-CMA-malleability could allow an adversary to substitute a different valid signature for the same authorization (potentially defeating per-signature revocation lists or signature-pinning audit invariants). LAMPS is right for LAMPS; Benten needs to be honest that LAMPS-as-used-in-Benten has a residual gap for the SUF-CMA-sensitive subset of use cases. That residual gap is the honest content of caveat #7.

objection_5.statement: Wouldn't surfacing SUF-CMA-omission in the blog create FUD — readers will conclude 'Benten chose a broken combiner'?
objection_5.response: Two reasons no. (a) Cryptographer-readers already know SUF-CMA is a real property, that hybrid-sig combiners that preserve it are an active research area, and that LAMPS chose EUF-CMA-only for principled reasons (X.509/CMS context); they will read 'SUF-CMA-omitted by design with named alternatives tracked' as competent disclosure, not as 'broken.' (b) Non-cryptographer-readers do not parse 'SUF-CMA' as a load-bearing term and will skip the caveat the way they skip other technical caveats — same as 'AEAD nonce-reuse is a known hazard' in TLS docs does not create FUD about TLS. The risk is asymmetric in the OTHER direction: shipping the blog WITHOUT the disclosure, then being publicly corrected by a Bird-of-Prey author or LAMPS WG participant, creates HIGH FUD ('Benten made unsubstantiated claims about combiner properties; can we trust their other technical claims?').
